tier_reason: On the pages I could open, the claims are first-party summaries: the README says 'up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn', and docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst and CHANGELOG v0.4.0 say 'up to 2x speedup over FlashTP'. The public harness tests/benchmark.py times e3nn, cue and oeq, and the docs state an A100-SXM-80GB, but no per-problem numbers, compiler or flags were visible, so the tier is C. The peer-reviewed SIAM ACDA25 paper (arXiv 2501.13986) would support B, but I saw its abstract only as WebSearch snippets because arXiv is egress-blocked.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 170 stars, 17 forks (github.com page, 2026-10-03); pip package 'openequivariance'; works with MACE and NequIP
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'We provide up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn' and performance 'on par with the latest version of NVIDIA cuEquivariance'; docs/index.rst: 'up to an order of magnitude speedup over e3nn and competitive performance with NVIDIA's cuEquivariance'. Docs (tests_and_benchmarks.rst) and CHANGELOG v0.4.0: 'up to 2x speedup over FlashTP's fused kernels'. Paper abstract (SIAM ACDA25, arXiv 2501.13986; WebSearch snippet only, paper not opened): fused kernels give up to 4.5x forward and 3x (another snippet says 3.5x) backward speedup over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn, and up to 5.3x (another snippet: 5.4x) MACE inference speedup over the original unoptimized version. One snippet also gives 5.3x over e3nn and 1.5x over cuEquivariance in FP32, and 6.6x and 1.43x in FP64. The snippet figures disagree between paper versions and need checking against the PDF.

notes: Accurate record; only the star count and the claimed_speedup text changed (paper-abstract figures added and marked as snippet only). This is a B candidate: once arxiv.org/abs/2501.13986 (or the SIAM ACDA25 version, DOI 10.1137/1.9781611978759.3) can be opened, check the per-problem e3nn and cuEquivariance figures and retier.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D to C. The independent preprint 'Speeding Up MACE: Low-Precision Tricks for Equivariant Force Fields' (arXiv 2510.23621) compares MACE's e3nn and cuEquivariance backends, and its abstract says cuEquivariance 'reduces inference latency by about 3x'. Two WebSearch snippets agree on this, but arXiv is egress-blocked, so methodology and hardware were not visible. The repo itself carries only an e3nn-vs-cuEquivariance timing cell with no stored output (docs/tutorials/pytorch/MACE.rst).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent study (arXiv 2510.23621, abstract seen via WebSearch snippets only, paper not opened): cuEquivariance 'reduces inference latency by about 3x' for MACE compared with the e3nn backend. Repo: no numbers. The MACE tutorial cell (docs/tutorials/pytorch/MACE.rst) prints 'Speedup: {e3nn_avg/cuet_avg}x' but stores no output; one WebSearch summary said the rendered docs.nvidia.com tutorial shows 5.6x for the channelwise tensor product, but a second targeted search did not confirm it and docs.nvidia.com is egress-blocked, so that figure is unverified. CHANGELOG '~3x' (JAX v0.3.0 vs Torch v0.2.0) and 'up to 2x' (uniform 1d kernel) compare cuEquivariance with its own earlier releases.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 441 stars, 43 forks (github.com page, 2026-10-03); NVIDIA library named in the README as accelerating DiffDock, MACE, Allegro and NequIP; a backend option in MACE
corrections.caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the independent arXiv 2510.23621 abstract (about 3x MACE inference latency versus e3nn) was read through WebSearch because arxiv.org is egress-blocked; methodology, GPU and precision were not visible. docs.nvidia.com was also egress-blocked, and the repo's MACE tutorial timing cell (1000 nodes, 10000 edges, multiplicity 128, float32, 1000 timed repetitions) stores no output. The tutorial itself notes 'our kernels tend to have best performance for very large input sizes'. The repo's Python frontends are Apache-2.0 ('All files hosted in this repository are subject to the Apache 2.0 license'), but the CUDA kernels ship as separate pip packages (cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12/-cu13, cuequivariance-ops-jax-*) under the proprietary 'NVIDIA Math Libraries SDK' license agreement (pypi.org metadata: 'Other/Proprietary License'), which forbids reverse engineering and derivative works, so usability is 'mixed'. Other independent measurements exist: OpenEquivariance's peer-reviewed ACDA25 paper and harness (tests/benchmark.py) time cuEquivariance against e3nn; per its abstract snippets, OpenEquivariance's fused kernels beat cuEquivariance by up to 4.5x forward. Vendor-only figures would cap at C.

notes: Upgraded D to C (verdict 'confirm' per the upgrade rule) because the independent arXiv 2510.23621 abstract gives about 3x MACE inference latency versus e3nn; seen as a WebSearch snippet only. Confirmed the proprietary license on the kernel pip package, so 'mixed' stands. A retier to B needs that paper (or the OpenEquivariance ACDA25 paper's cuE-vs-e3nn columns) to be opened.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D to C. The first-party Hazy Research blog post (hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2024-11-28-tk-mlx, egress-blocked, seen through a WebSearch snippet restricted to that domain) says the attention kernel is 'within +-15% of MLX' and the GEMM is '~9% faster on most sizes'. The repo carries the matching timing scripts (ThunderMittens/kernels/time_gemm.py, time_attn.py), but there are no stored results and compiler, flags and chip are not stated in the repo.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Hazy Research blog post 'ThunderMittens For Your ThunderKittens' (WebSearch snippet only; page egress-blocked): the attention kernel is 'within +-15% of MLX's implementation' (not a clear win) and the GEMM is '~9% faster on most sizes' than MLX's matmul. The repo stores no results; time_gemm.py and time_attn.py print GFLOPS for 'mlx' and 'tk' side by side.
corrections.hardware: Apple M2 Pro per blog snippets (the post describes the M2 Pro's ~200 GB/s bandwidth and ~6.5 TFLOPs); the repo does not name the chip, and the snippets do not show whether every timing ran on it.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are snippet only from the first-party blog post (hazyresearch.stanford.edu was egress-blocked), so the tier is no higher than C. The gain is modest: GEMM ~9% over mx.matmul, and attention is only on par (+-15%) with mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention. The repo has no LICENSE file of its own (only the vendored MLX tree is MIT), so the ThunderMittens code is reference-only. The repo history is two commits, both 'revive thundermittens' on 2025-08-26, after the repository had disappeared (ThunderKittens issue #132). Benchmark quirks in time_attn.py: the 'tk' warmup loop calls MLX's SDPA instead of the ThunderMittens kernel, scale=1 is passed to MLX SDPA while the TK kernel takes no scale, each iteration calls mx.eval (launch overhead included), and correctness is not checked. time_gemm.py warms up both kernels correctly. 24 stars, but the ThunderKittens README lists it as the Apple Silicon sibling of ThunderKittens and HipKittens.

notes: Upgraded D to C on a first-party blog claim seen as a domain-restricted WebSearch snippet (GEMM ~9% faster than MLX; attention within +-15%). The record is otherwise accurate: no license, stale (last commit 2025-08-26), 24 stars and 7 forks.
